Triggers.value: Water, flooding, or large bodies of water

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar
I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be on guard all the time
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I feel guilty for surviving when others did not

vignette:
Amina is a 20-year-old pharmacist who came to treatment exhausted, watchful, and ashamed of how small her life had become. She grew up in an African immigrant family in the United States and had been in a steady relationship for the past year, but since the trauma she had felt increasingly unreachable to the people closest to her. During a period of detention in which she was tortured, one of the most terrifying elements was the way control was stripped from her moment by moment. She was restrained, forced into positions she could not change, and threatened around water, with flooding and the sound and sight of it becoming fused in her mind with helplessness. She remembers raised voices giving orders, arguments breaking out nearby, and the sick certainty that whenever someone else decided what happened to her body, she had no protection at all. Even now, what she can describe comes in fragments; much of it feels unsayable to her, as if the worst parts never formed into words.

In the months after, ordinary situations began to carry the force of the detention room. At work in the pharmacy, if a customer started arguing at the counter or a supervisor told her she had to do something immediately, she felt her chest lock and her thoughts narrow. Passing a street after heavy rain, seeing standing water in a parking lot, or glimpsing a deep reflecting pool could pull up the same dread. In those moments she did not simply remember in a narrative way. Her body seemed to take over, and she felt herself pulled back into the position she had been held in during the torture, tense and braced as if movement were impossible. What frightened her was that the memory came as broken pieces and physical sensations rather than a complete story; the missing parts made it feel even less controllable.

These moments also confirmed what she had come to believe about herself and the world. When she was confronted by arguments or by being told what to do, she was seized not only by fear but by the conviction that she had to be on guard all the time. She had come to believe that if she let herself think directly about what happened, she would not be able to handle it, that she might come apart completely. Water and forceful voices carried another sting: she would find herself thinking of people who did not survive and feeling, with abrupt cruelty toward herself, that she deserved to suffer when others had not had the chance to live. Over time, those meanings made the triggers feel broader and more potent; it was no longer only a specific kind of water or a specific tone of voice, but any sign that someone else might take control.

Because she feared what the reminders would unleash, Amina began arranging her days around not setting anything off. She avoided evening routines that reminded her of sleep, lingering in bright rooms with her phone or extra chores because bedtime had become associated with nightmares. At work she found reasons to let colleagues handle agitated customers, and in public she would quietly change aisles or leave stores if she saw someone who resembled one of the people involved in her detention. When guilt surged, she sometimes leaned into it, telling herself she deserved the discomfort and should not seek relief. These habits gave her brief relief, but they also kept the trauma unspoken and unprocessed; the more she pushed away thoughts and situations connected to it, the more the memory stayed in pieces, returning as bodily states rather than words.

Her beliefs fed a state of constant readiness. Because she was convinced she must stay on guard, she scanned every room for signs of danger and could not settle anywhere until she had identified an exit. She did this automatically now in the pharmacy, in restaurants with her boyfriend, even in the waiting room before sessions. At night she struggled to fall asleep because staying alert felt safer than drifting off. This vigilance sharpened the trauma's hold on her mind: when she was keyed up and searching for threat, the fragmented sensory memories came faster, and the physical reenactment was more likely. Each episode seemed to prove to her that she really was in danger and that letting down her guard would be reckless.

The strategies she used to cope tightened that pattern further. By avoiding people who looked similar to those involved and steering around water, arguments, or situations where she might be directed by others, she never had the chance to learn that these moments in the present were not the torture itself. Her world narrowed into a map of possible danger zones, and she entered each new place already planning escape routes. Sleep deprivation made her even more reactive, and the constant scanning left her jumpy and mentally worn thin. In that depleted state, the trauma remained hard to put into words, surfacing instead as flashes, bodily postures, and blank spaces that she could not fill in.

What finally brought Amina to seek help was a recent incident at the pharmacy when an angry customer began shouting about a prescription delay. She froze, felt her body lock into that old position, and had to leave the counter abruptly while a coworker covered for her. Later that week, after avoiding sleep for most of the night and checking the exits repeatedly at her boyfriend's apartment, she told him she was scared she was becoming impossible to live with. She came in fearing that if she ever stopped guarding herself, the memories would overwhelm her, but also hoping that she might learn how to live without every argument, order, or patch of water feeling like a return to captivity.
